subject: dumboOctopus
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: dumbo octopus.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through unexpected artistic styles for this dumbo octopus—maybe art-deco cloisonné, ukiyo-e woodblock, or stained glass bioluminescent lantern—while keeping in mind its key features: the bulbous pink mantle, ear-like fins, side-set eyes, and webbed suckered arms.

Weighing clockwork brass automaton against Delftware porcelain, I'm settling on the latter: a white-glazed figurine with cobalt blue painted ornaments and gilt accents, giving the pink dumbo octopus an unexpected ceramic elegance with scrollwork fins, tulip-motif webbing, and dark cobalt eyes with highlights.

For pose, I'm having the creature rest naturally with its mantle raised and arms splayed outward touching the floor, mimicking how a real dumbo octopus settles on the seafloor, sized around 0.3m wide and 0.2m tall. Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure—root body joint, a spine chain up to the mantle and head, eye joints, eight tentacle-role arm chains with webbing between them, and two ear-like fin chains on the mantle, trying to decide the right role name for those fins.

I'm adding a hidden beak joint tucked under the arm crown near the mouth, and orienting the whole creature to face forward with the bulbous mantle positioned above and behind the head, eyes on the sides, fins angled up-outward, and arms radiating from the front-bottom in a splayed semicircle around the mouth.

Now I'm working out the arm splay angles symmetrically around the forward direction and tracing each arm's path from the mouth point outward and down until it lies along the floor, tapering the radius from base to tip and letting the tip curl up slightly off the surface.

For webbing, I'm connecting adjacent arms with thin membrane surfaces covering the inner 60% of each arm's length, cycling through all neighboring pairs including the rear ones to complete the umbrella shape.

I'll pass chain A as the bone for smooth blending between edges. For thickness, I'm thinking the membrane should be thin (~0.006) but slightly raised near the body rather than lying totally flat, so the web drapes like a tent between the arms rather than creating a flat skirt that could look odd near the floor.

Now I'm sketching out the mantle's spine as a loft: a catmull-rom path running from the front of the head to the rear, with elliptical radius values tapering along the body to give it a rounded, tapering profile.

I'll keep smooth shading for the body with 12 sides for a glossy porcelain look. For the rig, I'm planning a single root joint ("body", spine role) with a mantle chain parented to it, and a head joint at the front of the mantle for the eyes to follow.

For the mantle chain I'll just use count:4 and let it auto-name the joints mantle1 through mantle4 rather than fussing over explicit names. For the eyes, since dumbo octopus eyes sit large on the sides of the head, I'm thinking they'd work best as decals placed on the head sweep surface.

Still working out the eyeball decal...

Settling on 0.045 for the decal size. Now thinking through the fins/ears: attaching them at the upper-rear sides of the mantle pointing outward like flapping elephant ears, considering whether to build them as a membrane between root and tip edges versus a simpler bone chain extrusion with ribbed decoration for structure.

I'll go with a 3-joint "finL" chain extruded as a tapered ear shape, oriented with the outward axis and tilted upward axis for the fin plane, mirrored for the left side.

From the front view, the ears should look like round paddle flaps sticking out to the sides, so I want the fin's flat surface facing forward rather than lying flat horizontally. I'm setting up the local axes so the outward direction tilts up slightly, the second axis points mostly upward with a bit of inward tilt, and their cross product gives the thickness direction facing forward.

Adding ring ornaments and ribs...

Now I'm sketching the ear fin outline point by point, aiming for exaggerated dumbo-style proportions with a wide span of about 0.36 relative to body size, and working out a constant taper thickness for the fin edge.

For painting the fin, I'm computing an approximate center and radius so the cobalt rim coloring lands correctly along the outline. Since the arms rest flat on the floor, I'm deciding suckers would be hidden underneath, so instead I'll add cobalt decorative dashes or dot motifs along the tops of the arms.

I'm placing cobalt diamond dots periodically along the dorsal centerline of each arm, then adding small white sucker rings along the visible lateral sides at an angle, looping through each of the eight arms to place them manually since the sweep function only gives the dorsal path.

Rather than overload the part count with suckers on both sides of all arms, I'm rethinking the pose: letting the arm tips curl upward at rest so the underside suckers peek out charmingly, which also keeps the sucker placement limited to just the curled portion of each arm for visibility and part efficiency.

Still designing the sucker geometry...

I realize the body needs to sit higher above the arms so they emerge from its underside properly—adjusting the mantle's centerline and radius so the bottom sits around y≈0.045, with arm roots buried in a tighter ring near y=0.05 and radius 0.015-0.04, tapering outward and down from there.

Looking at overall proportions, the arms plus fins push the total span past 0.4, which is too large for a real Dumbo octopus around 20-30cm, so I'm scaling the whole model down with a constant factor to bring the overall span closer to 0.30.

I'll just scale by 0.8 with a helper function, accepting the resulting size won't be perfectly realistic but stays reasonable. Now I'm working out the body height and fin placement under this scale, then mapping out each arm's path points by azimuth angle.

Each arm radiates outward from a center point near the mantle base, with points placed at increasing radial distances and decreasing heights so the arms sweep down and back from the body.

Using 8-sided circles for the arms to keep them lightweight, and scaling rear arms slightly thinner than front ones for a more natural taper. I'm ordering the arms by azimuth angle around both sides and pairing adjacent arms to create the webbing between them.

For the webbing itself, I'm taking a partial slice of each arm's edge path to form the membrane boundary, then adding a light-blue wash with thin cobalt scalloped lines near the trailing rim and small accent dots scattered across the surface.

I'm thinking about whether the web should sag or drape between the arms, deciding to keep it conical and flat near the root even where it intersects the body. For the mouth, I'll add a small hidden beak under the web with separate upper and lower jaw cones, mimicking a real dumbo octopus's mouth placement.

I'll nudge the beak to poke out slightly in front of the body, above the web, even if it partially overlaps. Then I need a siphon—a small funnel-like tube sprouting from the underside near the head, angled forward-down on the right side.

For the overall dumbo identity, I want to nail the big round ear fins, lateral eyes, and webbed arms, plus maybe add a cobalt-painted Delft ornamental band like a tulip motif across the mantle for decorative flair.

I'm thinking through the porcelain paint scheme now: white glaze on top with a cooler blue-grey shadow underneath and a coral blush near the cheeks, topped off with a hero Delft medallion decal (floral rosette/tulip) placed on the mantle crown, plus a cobalt wave-pattern border swept around the rear and a dotted ring band circling the mantle.

Now I'm figuring out the texture/decal list — eye, medallion, maybe tiny cirri-like projections along the arms, a wave band, scroll decals on the fins, and a small coral blush decal near the eye, considering whether to add a hidden maker's mark on the belly too.

I'm adding a glossy specular highlight decal on the mantle to simulate porcelain shine — a slightly bluish-cream base color with a pure white arc for the glossy streak, keeping the Dumbo octopus's bioluminescence out of scope since the style is porcelain, and leaning toward defining a gilt metal color directly rather than importing a clockwork metal kit to limit risk.

Setting up imports from the agentic-3js-builder module...

Now I'm defining the Delftware palette: whites and creams for the glaze, cobalt blues at varying depths, a coral accent, and gilt gold tones for trim details.

I'm setting up scaling helpers to convert design-space coordinates and radii into model-space units, keeping authored absolute points and radii consistent while letting hit-based positions derive naturally. Starting to build the model skeleton for the dumbo octopus figure.

Mapping out the mantle shape as a bulbous profile that rises toward the back and tapers at the head, with a path of points and corresponding radii defining its silhouette.

I'm chaining joints along that mantle path, parented to the body, then sweeping a shell geometry through those joints using a radius function with rounded caps to form the smooth dumbo-like body.

The length-to-width ratio looks too elongated, so I'm adjusting the path points and radii to pull the body shape toward something more compact and rounded.

Now I'm writing the shader for the shell surface, blending a warm white highlight at the top into a cooler blue-grey shadow underneath, with a coral blush worked into the lower front to give it that dumbo-pink character.

I'm also adding subtle speckled flecks using noise to mimic a Delft-style glaze texture, keeping the measurements consistent in meters since the model space is already properly scaled. Then I'm setting up the head joint attached to the body at a defined position and orientation, establishing the role as "head" for the rig hierarchy.

For the eyes, I'm riding them on the head bone so they stay rigid rather than deforming with the mantle's skin weights, then placing sphere geometries symmetrically on either side using a radial hit-test against the head surface to position them correctly along the azimuth, with a small embed offset and scaled dimensions for the eyeball glaze material.

Figuring out the eye placement...

I'll keep the eye design mostly symmetrical with just a small eyelash flick on top, using default up orientation, and binding the decal's weights to the head bone. Now I'm sketching the eye SVG itself—a cobalt ring for the iris with a deep inner circle and pupil detail inside a 100x100 viewBox.

Adjusting decal sizing so the iris wraps roughly 70% of the eyeball's visible side while leaving white sclera showing at the rim, then adding a thin gilt torus ring around the eye socket itself.

I'm adding lash spikes arranged in a ring around the eyeball's upper arc using cobalt-colored spikes, then starting to plan coral blush decals under each eye on the mantle.

Now I'm sketching the fins as chained segments extending outward from a point near the body's side, building each fin as a curved path offset along x and y from its base point.

I'm deciding how to name and parent these fin joints, considering whether to explicitly attach them to a mantle joint or let them inherit the nearest bone automatically -- opting to just rely on the closest joint since the base point sits near the mantle anyway.

Now I'm setting up the fin extrusion, defining its direction vectors, scaled thickness, bevel, and paint, while binding its bone to the fin chain's first joint. I'm also thinking about how the fin root should sit flush against the sloped mantle surface rather than floating off a flat base point.

Still writing rim sweep logic...

Still shaping the ear outline...

Still writing shader math...

For the arms, I'm designing a paint function that countershades the top with glaze versus coral underside based on surface normal, adds cobalt dash stripes along the limb axis, and lays a diamond pattern down the spine.

Building the arm construction function, computing direction and perpendicular vectors per angle, then laying out the control points along the arm's length with curl offsets...

I'm checking that the radius values taper correctly along the arm profile, and reasoning through how the curl direction exposes the sucker-lined underside when viewed from the front.

Now I'm setting up the arm chains using a Catmull-Rom spline through the control points, naming each joint with a consistent pattern so the parenting and chain count line up correctly with the body root.

For the arm sweep, I'm applying a tapered radius array along each chain to shape the tentacle thickness smoothly. For the webbing between arms, I'm figuring out how to slice each arm's curve path and bind the connecting edges to a shared bone so both sides follow the same movement.

Writing edge construction code...

I'm thinking through membrane placement to keep the web root hidden inside the body, starting around t=0.05, and planning the paint thickness, scallop shape, and row detail. Then I'm working out sucker placement along each arm from t=0.55 to 0.95, spacing six per arm at the belly angle with appropriate radius and embed scale for the torus shapes.

Writing sucker geometry...

Actually simpler: instead of adding a separate gilt bead part, I can bake the gold tip directly into the paint function, making the arm tube return a gold color near its endpoint so the tip looks capped in gilt without extra geometry.

Finishing the small tube geometry, then moving to the jaw joint and beak shapes, defining a jaw joint anchored near the head's front and setting up upper beak as a tapered cone from a base point toward a forward tip.

I'm checking whether the beak tip actually clears the body's cap sphere by computing the sphere's radius at that height, confirming it protrudes slightly beyond the front surface, and verifying where the facial web attaches relative to the beak root.

Checking the gap between the left and right root angles, I see the web covers it and the beak sits just above the web's edge, like a small gilded beak perched over it. Now I'm setting up a ray cast from the mantle top to place a medallion decal onto the skin surface.

I'm orienting the decal so its drawn "up" direction points toward the rear when viewed from the front, then sketching out the medallion itself as a Delft-style tulip and rosette design with a double cobalt ring, dotted border, central eight-petal flower, four leaves, and scroll corners on a transparent background.

Writing SVG code...

Defining the band helper function...

I realize the joint at that position would cross right through the medallion, so I need to shift the band positions forward or back to avoid the overlap, picking a joint whose z-coordinate sits clear of the medallion's span.

I'll place the rings using a loop oriented along the mantle's tangent direction at specific parameter points, estimating the cross-section radius at each location to size the bands appropriately — putting them around t=0.86-0.93 where the mantle narrows, with beads slightly before at t=0.895.

Now I want to add subtle Delft-style decoration: scattering small pale dots across the shell using a cell-based noise function to create a sprig pattern, plus a glossy highlight streak for shine.

I'm also placing a highlight crescent on the mantle and eyes for glassy reflections, and considering whether to add decorative cirri textures along the arms, tallying up the texture count so far (eye, medallion, blush, highlight) against the paint layers I still need for shell, fin, arm, web, and gilt accents.

For the fifth texture, I'm sketching a small Delft-style maker's mark—a cobalt tulip monogram with "D·O" lettering—to place near the tail on the mantle's rear underside, giving it a collector's-piece feel.

I'm skipping the "CIRRUS" arm label but considering tiny gilt pupils for the eyes. With the texture count settled, I'm thinking through a few more decorative touches—raised gilt bands at the arm roots—while deciding against extras like inlaid dots or trailing pearls that would overcrowd the design.

Each arm gets a gilt bracelet ring built from a closed sweep around the arm's chain, placed near where the arms meet the floor, plus a cobalt ring further along. I need to check these bracelets don't clash with the web membrane spanning the structure.

Tallying up parts now: body, mantle, eyes with lashes, blush, highlights, bands with beads, fins, arms with their sweeps/bracelets/suckers, webs, beak, funnel — roughly 140 total, comfortably under the 180 cap, so I can add a few extras like a gilt eyebrow dot, cheeks, and maybe small pearl-like sprigs on the webs.

I'm weighing whether to add a gilt flange torus ring where each fin meets the body, but the orientation mismatch between fin plane and hit normal makes that fiddly, so I'll skip it and instead consider decaling a tulip motif onto the front face of each fin instead of hand-painting it.

I need to work out the decal placement: both fins' front faces should face +Z so the tulip reads correctly, and I'm figuring out how to position the decal anchor point right at the fin's front surface, possibly by raycasting from in front of the fin toward it to find the exact surface point.

I'll orient the tulip's up vector along the outline's tilted y-axis, and keep ribs restricted to the outer rim zone so they don't clash with the tulip painted in the center. The tulip SVG itself needs stem, leaves, and three petals in cobalt-on-white with pale shading, plus a separate eye texture at a larger viewbox. Now I'm assembling the full code and double-checking the type declarations stay loose enough for the module to run cleanly.

I'm writing a typed helper that throws if a required value is null, then setting up positions and orientations for sticking geometry onto eye hits using the skin's `around`/`at` lookup. Writing imports and setup code...

Still writing shell paint logic...

Settling on 0.16 for the sprig dot threshold, restricted to the mantle only. I'm now defining an arm paint function that wraps angle differences and blends gilt flat tones with coral and glaze colors based on vertical position and thresholds.

I want the underside coral gradient to fade correctly against the white sides, and I'm checking the diamond pattern logic so it only renders on the top-facing portion of each arm, with a smaller glaze center dot nested inside a cobalt diamond. Also renaming the unused parameter to avoid lint warnings before moving on to the web paint function.

Now I'm working out the festoon pattern for the webbing between arms, placing rows of cobalt dots at regular intervals along the arm length and centering them across the width, trying to get the spacing and dot radius right relative to the cell count.

I'm defining the pale line threshold and the web rim coloring near the edge, then setting up a gilt mottle texture (gold tones) for beak, rim, bracelets and beads, plus a flat gilt variant for other uses.

Now I'm picking a flat eye-ball color and fin paint, then generating the ear outline points by looping around an ellipse with a wobble factor to create scallops before pushing rounded coordinates into the array.

I'm checking the fin dimensions against the mantle size — making sure the clipped base edge doesn't self-intersect and verifying the overall proportions stay reasonable relative to the body height.

Checking the extrude axes — the fin's local x/y basis leans outward and up from the ear base, so the ear center sits properly outside the body, but I need to verify whether the top corner of the fin outline actually clears the body surface at that height.

Working through the fin's control points and basis vectors...

Still writing sweep and fin decal logic...

Verified orthogonality holds for the mirrored basis too. For visibility I'll add a second decal on the back face so the tulip symmetric pattern shows from both sides, giving four decals total. Now I'm writing a helper function that sweeps a pentagon-sided band around a loop lifted from the mantle curve, used for beads and bands.

Checking that the bead-placement function works by walking along a path and placing bead geometry at each frame, and confirming the skin needs to be built after the shell so later parts like eyes aren't missed.

For the eyes, I'm sketching symmetric placement by sampling skin points around a facial reference, attaching sphere geometry scaled non-uniformly per axis and bound to the head bone. I'm unsure whether the scale parameter accepts an array directly, so I'm reasoning through how the part/stick signature likely handles vector-style scaling.

I'm sizing the eyeball radius relative to head width to gauge how much it should bulge from the mantle surface, then working out how to place a pupil decal on the eye using an offset helper that nudges a point along a normal direction by some distance.

Next I'm sketching the eyelid ring attachment — sizing its radius and tube thickness so it sits just outside the eyeball's surface at the attachment point.

For the lashes, I'm placing them in a ring pattern around the ball's center, spanning an angular range with a tilt, spawning small cobalt spikes at each position along that arc.

Now I'm setting up blush decals, finding a cheek anchor point near the head and preparing to place a blush decal there sized appropriately.

I'm skipping a mouth decoration and instead placing a maker's mark on the rear cap, casting a ray from behind to find the hit point near the top of the rear. I need to check that this mark doesn't overlap too much with the surrounding bands near the rear tip region.

Let me shift the mark slightly lower on the rear dome where it clears the rings, confirming it fits within the dome's radius and orienting it upright for viewing from behind.

That settles bead positioning at t=0.84, placed on the rear dome. Now I'm defining the arm segments with their azimuth angles and lengths, then working out how to position each arm's root point in 3D space using sine and cosine of the azimuth relative to a center offset.

Working out the perpendicular curl direction and radius/height/lateral offset points for each arm segment...

For the final webbing pair I'm wrapping L4 to R4 across the back, keeping root-to-tip edges consistent, with a scallop width around 0.18. I'm sampling the arm chain at several parameter points to build the curve for the web edges, checking that the chain point type is compatible with the catmull spline input.

Now I'm setting a small web thickness and figuring out sucker placement along the arm sweep, planning six suckers spaced between t=0.5 and 0.88 with scaling based on the local radius so they shrink appropriately toward the tip, passing that scale as a number to the stick geometry call.

For the bracelets, I'm placing gilt and cobalt rings at specific points along the chain, deriving ring radius from the chain's local tube radius plus a small offset, and accounting for the octagonal cross-section so the circumscribed vertices sit correctly around the arm's centerline before sweeping a small decorative tube through them.

I'm now checking that no decals collide — fins, eyes, and any painted details stay clear of each other — and settling the joint hierarchy, confirming the head joint carries no extra geometry beyond the eyes, and defining the body joint as the root spine before building out the mantle chain.

Then I'm verifying the shell sweep follows the mantle joints smoothly without linking to the head bone, and double-checking the floor clearance math for the arms and webbing to make sure every lowest point sits just above or at ground level.

Checking that the octagonal tessellation keeps bottoms exactly aligned with path minus radius, and that catmull-rom overshoot near P3-P4 only dips about a millimeter, which is within tolerance. Then estimating overall body height by tracing the path and radius near the top to figure out where the fins peak above the body.

I'm now defining the fin geometry for each side, computing root offsets from the mantle surface along perpendicular axes, then building a short catmull-rom chain for each fin with named joints parented to the nearest mantle joint, using wing as the role. Writing fin bone chain...

Writing fin paint shader logic...

The outline wobbles between radius 0.95 and 1.05 to create a scalloped edge, with the cobalt rim thickness varying 3-8mm near d>0.9, plus a gilt rim sweep layered over it. For the center, I'm sizing the tulip decal to roughly 5-6cm wide so it fits within the pink d<0.5 region.

Now I'm sketching the eye SVG with a layered iris: an outer navy ring, an inner darker circle, a gold stroke, radial sun-like rays, a dark pupil offset slightly downward, and a white highlight ellipse rotated for a glossy look.

Then I'm defining the blush as a soft coral ellipse with subtle darker slashes and an inner lighter layer, and starting on a crescent-shaped white highlight path for added shine.

Now I'm sketching the medallion with programmatic petals, and the mark icon using a cobalt-outlined circle with bold serif initials "D·O" centered inside it. For the tulip, I'm drawing a cobalt stem line and starting on the leaf paths.

Generating medallion petals and rings...

Still placing the funnel geometry...

Now I just need to set up the meta export with name and description, then write out the final code carefully, double-checking the type signatures for things like the generic placeholder and the hit result returned from the positioning call.

Writing the arm construction loop...

Still defining tentacle geometry...

Still writing membrane loop...

Now I'm sketching the beak structure, adding a jaw joint and spikes for upper and lower beak pieces attached to head and jaw bones respectively, working out what it means for a spike's direction argument to be null.

I'm double-checking that the colors stay within the flat-color limit and that the helper functions and constants I need (cells, noise, smoothstep, mix, paint, mottle, DEG) are all properly exported from the SDK before continuing to work out the highlight code around the skin.

Still writing decal placements...

Also adding a stick for the lid ring torus, rotated so its axis runs along Y, and checking sphere geometries for consistency.

I'm setting up a shared eyeball sphere geometry and a smaller bead sphere geometry so they can be reused across parts rather than recreated each time. The names and flat-shading options on parts aren't critical, so I'm skipping those refinements and moving toward writing the final code.
